---
type: video-summary
video_id: 81CC-uLrOtE
title: "SSAC17: Ball Don't Lie: The Future of Basketball Analytics"
event: SSAC17 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Barry brudney (host, caption spelling), Zach low (moderator, caption spelling), Luis skola (caption spelling), Mike Zaron (caption spelling), Vin Alro (caption spelling), Dean Oliver, Sue (first name only, [59:29])]
topics: [basketball, sports-science, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A moderated panel of a current player, a front-office executive, a former player and coach, a WNBA guard and an analytics executive discusses where basketball analytics goes next. The recurring argument is that tracking data is most useful when it produces small, specific, coachable findings (who gets hung up on screens, how often hands go up) and when it reaches players in a form they can use. The panel also covers wearables, tests that players can train for, how to judge coaches, and officiating data. The speakers repeatedly stress that human judgment and communication decide whether a number gets used.

## Key claims

- Camera tracking data is most valuable for small defensive details (screen handling, closeouts, hand position), not for confirming large strategic trends. [02:44]
- Every screen can now be identified and reviewed, which lets analysts speak in coaches' terms. [03:15]
- Giving a coach the percentage of ways an opponent creates a shot lets a staff decide which version to concede. [04:17]
- A panelist argued that a small fix, such as one high hand, can decide a game because runs happen fast. [05:19]
- Data is a way to build a relationship with a player, but it has to be delivered simply; the panel says players are far behind coaches and analysts in understanding numbers. [09:24]
- Seeing percentages about yourself can become a mental problem (a player described being told which direction she shoots better and then overthinking it). [10:25]
- Some panelists said numbers help a team know the opponent better than they help a player know himself. [11:25]
- Some players can take many items and others only one or two, so staff must know the individual. [11:56]
- A panelist told young players they will have to understand analytics eventually, so they should start early. [12:27]
- For acquisitions, the useful question is fit: whether a player's skills overlap with or add to existing players. [19:36]
- A panelist argued against combining skill metrics into one good-or-bad score; instead, keep the skill metrics and weigh them by the team's system. [20:06]
- Fit analysis can be done quickly if the groundwork is built before the deadline. [21:08]
- Psychological or neurological tests should be tested against on-court results before being trusted; vendors who say they can quantify them need checking. [25:12]
- Physical numbers need context: compare a strong, high-jumping player with another who rebounds more. [25:42]
- A team's hand-coordination test matched its deflection chart, but players who trained for the test rose in the rankings without rising in deflections. [28:15]
- Training for a test exclusively changes the result without translating to the game. [28:45]
- Some teams are growing skeptical of wearables and asking whether a device is worth its cost. [29:45]
- One panelist trusts sport scientists by default but wants to confirm they cause no harm and keep looking. [31:16]
- A practice described as a "light" half-court session was tracked as much harder than a full-court one, and the player said this kind of information is crucial. [32:48]
- Perceived exertion compared with tracking data could indicate whether a player is getting hurt, if one player's rating drifts from the group. [33:50]
- A panelist is willing to wear a device in games and argued analytics tools only need to be a little better than what came before, not perfect. [35:21]
- Players who dismiss a mismatch between feel and data are common, and some may use the data as an excuse. [36:53]
- A panelist said team and player interests are nearly always aligned on this data, so the excuse problem is not a reason to withhold it. [37:23]
- Wearable data identified a drill coaches had called a throwaway as very tiring. [38:26]
- One panelist said most "new" ideas from outsiders were tried and discarded earlier. [39:30]
- A panelist proposed game-format practices with tracked stats scaled up to build bigger samples for lineup analysis. [41:02]
- A shoot-around is disliked by some panelists, who said sleep matters more. [42:34]
- Wide-open three-point range extension is described as becoming common in the league. [44:07]
- Coaching quality is hard to measure; indirect measures such as player development under a coach do not say why. [48:47]
- Coaching is a bundle of skills, some measurable (lineups) and some human (teaching). [50:49]
- The league's openness with teams about officiating process was praised, though calls will still anger teams. [56:56]
- Coaches track short-term patterns well, with a staff and bench computer; longer-term patterns are harder for human brains. [58:58]

## Numbers and definitions

- Panel length 45 minutes plus 15 minutes of Q&A. [00:42]
- A coach was told high hands were happening 10 percent of the time (an illustrative example). [04:48]
- The "80" and "2 minutes" in the run discussion are garbled in the captions; do not rely on them. [04:48]
- One panelist is 36. [10:55]
- Information can be pulled up within 5 minutes for most fit questions. [21:08]
- The draft-combine example questions: 90 cents in five coins, and how many balloons fit in a room (10,000 cited). [22:10]
- One player's team in Russia did tests for 30 seconds each; he played there 10 years. [26:13]
- Perceived exertion example: players rate a practice eight or nine while the coach thinks two. [33:19]
- 440 NBA players next year (as stated). [34:21]
- A panelist said team and player interests align 98 percent of the time. [37:23]
- Multiply tracked stats by four for a one-quarter scrimmage, by two for two quarters. [41:02]
- Shoot-around: the speaker said she believed the other 11 teams in her league have one. [42:04]
- Three-point range: 28 to 30 footers cited for two named players. [44:07]
- Russell Westbrook triple-double streak described as something not done in 50 years. [46:43]
- Of the 30 NBA coaches, a hypothetical person might class three as good, three as bad and not know 24. [51:20]
- Win Share and adjusted plus-minus per minute were suggested for MVP. [45:41]
- Perceived exertion (RPE) is defined by the panel as the player's rating of how hard a practice was. [33:19]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Optical player tracking (SportVU/camera data, "sport view" in the captions) for possessions and screens.
- Pick-and-roll coverage and screen quality analysis from tracking data.
- Wearable tracking (Zephyr, caption spelling) compared with perceived exertion.
- Test-the-test: validate non-basketball tests against on-court outcomes.
- Game-format practice to enlarge samples.
- Indirect coach evaluation via player development with and without a coach.
- Points per possession for youth-level video tracking.

## Limits and open questions

- Speaker attribution is unclear in the auto captions; many statements cannot be tied to a named panelist.
- Most evidence is anecdote; no sample sizes or results were shown for wearables, tests or practice formats.
- The panel did not resolve whether wearables improve outcomes; skepticism was acknowledged.
- A panelist's contractual limit prevented discussion of one team's front office. [16:05]
- Claims about player-team interest alignment (98 percent) are one panelist's view, not data.
- No research evidence was named for the coach-evaluation approach.

## Q&A

- MVP analytics: panelists named Win Share and adjusted plus-minus, and noted award voting is often based on a stat. [45:41]
- Analytics for youth and high school coaches: cheap video tools and points per possession. [47:47]
- How to measure coaches: indirect development measures and lineups; much remains unmeasured. [48:47]
- Officiating data: panelists praised league transparency and discussed adding a fourth referee. [55:55]
- Real-time data to coaches: staff track plays by hand or bench computer; coaches remember short-term patterns. [58:28]

## Summary

A presentation from a company that combines athlete tracking data with coaching video. The main speaker, a former college football graduate assistant, argues that data only matters if coaches understand it and believe it. He uses a personal story about missing bowl-game stats to show that analysts must know the limits of their data. He describes observed versus laboratory metrics, the value of consistent third-party data, and the need to validate new tracked metrics against film. He says staff should set thresholds, and analysts should earn trust by checking current decisions. The talk is a vendor presentation.

## Key claims

- The company's data pairs with coaching video, since coaches work in video. [02:06]
- Analysts must know the boundaries of their data; a missed bowl-game stat in a report cost the speaker and a colleague credibility with the head coach. [05:41]
- Metrics have long come in two kinds: observed (video, practice) and laboratory. [06:42]
- Some fields are empirical (down, distance) and others subjective (formation, personnel), and verbiage differs by staff. [08:14]
- Third-party data gives consistent definitions across teams. [09:46]
- A defined metric such as burn defender can save coaches large amounts of review time, at the cost of some false positives. [10:18]
- Coaches grew willing to use third-party data after comparing it with their own for about a year. [10:49]
- Staff buy-in decides whether findings are used. [12:23]
- Metrics must be accurate and precise, and must help win a game. [14:28]
- A researcher whose results cannot be explained to a coach does not matter to the coach. [15:30]
- Wearables allow metrics from practice and games rather than the laboratory. [16:01]
- Staff must decide the threshold that matters for a given sport and metric. [18:03]
- Coaches often get spreadsheets of tracking numbers that do not relate to their coaching points. [18:33]
- Load metrics can address within-game, weekly and seasonal preparation and injury risk, but coaches often do not understand them. [19:03]
- Players may resist if they fear the data shows they are out of shape. [19:34]
- The company validated a repeat-effort movement metric against hours of video. [20:35]
- A radar view overlays tracked speed on practice film, letting coaches pick color thresholds. [22:06]
- Specific film examples (a cut one way versus the other) make the data usable with athletes. [22:38]
- Buy-in needs to run from head coach to players. [23:09]
- Build the relationship by checking how the staff decides today and validating or invalidating it. [24:11]
- Many research papers will go unused if no team relates to them. [24:41]

## Numbers and definitions

- The speaker's story is dated 1996 (first year as graduate assistant), with a call in 2000. [02:36], [04:40]
- Report: a three-ring binder about an inch thick, several hundred pages. [03:38]
- The captions for the player's bowl-game line are garbled: five catches and a figure that reads "another hundred 38 yards." [03:38]
- Burn defender: defined as a receiver within two yards of the person who caught the ball. [10:18]
- 256 games and 40,000 plays for an NFL season; the captions say 87 results with "eight full false positives" (garbled). [10:18]
- Hockey example: heart rate above 165 beats per minute, a shift of 25 seconds, recovery in under 20 seconds versus two minutes on the bench. [17:32]
- Coaches and scouts watch video 10 to 14 hours a day. [20:35]
- The movement metric was developed over a year. [20:35]
- Radar-view example threshold of 12 miles an hour; the second figure ("80 miles hour") is garbled. [22:06]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Observed versus laboratory metrics.
- Peer-review test: accurate, precise, understandable to coaches, helps win.
- Validation of tracked metrics against video by staff.
- Radar view: tracked speed over practice film with staff-chosen thresholds.
- Third-party event data (a named provider appears in captions as "ProFootballFocus").

## Limits and open questions

- The talk is a vendor presentation; claims about the value of combining video and wearable data are the speaker's commercial view.
- No data, sample sizes or results were shown for any validation.
- Captions are very garbled in several passages (speed thresholds, false-positive counts, statistics).
- Names in the story may be misspelled. Adam "gay" in the captions was named as a former student and later a head coach of the Dolphins (caption spelling).
- Smart-ball and heart-rate examples are described as examples, not results.
- No Q&A was captured; the talk ends with applause. [25:11]

Four sports executives and a Wharton moderator talk about how cognitive bias affects front-office decisions. They agree that people are poor decision makers and discuss luck versus process, anchoring, loss aversion, regret, group think and owner influence. Practical tools they describe include writing a thesis and rereading it, reversing a trade, treating each decision as independent, and asking scouts to explain their weighting. They debate blending quantitative models with subjective scouting, how to judge scouts, and whether team chemistry causes winning. The panel is mostly anecdote from the speakers' own experience.

## Key claims

- A panelist said people are very poor at decisions and that even knowing about biases such as anchoring and loss aversion does not remove them. [02:34]
- Each decision should be treated as independent of earlier ones; a prior assumption about a college or region can mislead. [06:39]
- Good outcomes involve luck, and a right process can still produce a bad outcome. [07:41]
- Leaders should act as a corrective against over-praising good moves and over-grieving bad ones. [08:11]
- Over-correcting by thinking too much about bias can stifle a decision. [09:11]
- A secret grading ballot may give a false sense of independence because staff share the same training. [10:12]
- Model-versus-expert studies in other fields suggest added expertise can make a model worse; whether sports models are good enough to be improved is open. [11:46]
- Hands stay on the knobs because data is thin and does not know the future of a young player. [12:46]
- The first Moneyball-style draft was purely objective, and a panelist said he would not recommend that. [15:18]
- Subjective scouting became a data point in decisions once a quantitative colleague pushed for balance. [16:49]
- Some of the best analysts weigh analytics lower because they have seen where it misleads. [18:21]
- Predicting a young player's course is like predicting a stranger, so gather many data points about the person. [19:54]
- Scouts cannot be expected to predict a 17-year-old's ten-year result; ground-level information adds value. [20:56]
- A draftee's early performance in instruction or practice may reveal a lower pick as better, and a team should accept that. [22:28]
- Ordinal ranking of subjective qualities can aid decisions (a panelist cited Kahneman and a paper). [23:29]
- A firefighter example in the captions is used to argue that "gut" is accumulated information. [24:29]
- Ask scouts to explain how they weight things; share of an evaluation resting on one data point matters. [27:01]
- Test a strong claim as a hypothesis: the panelist had ten staff rate a player's ball handling on random video. [28:03]
- Passionate advocates are useful because they expose reasoning. [28:34]
- A panelist described clearing the slate with a new strategy, citing a 2011 trade of three players. [30:09]
- Write the argument down and reread it, or have someone else poke holes. [30:39]
- Write an investment thesis with confidence, set it aside two weeks, and reread. [31:10]
- Reverse every trade: would you do the other side? [31:41]
- A panelist described a hypothetical removal of a player to test whether regret was driving resistance to a trade. [32:44]
- Owners' hints shift staff decisions quickly, and a panelist said hunkering down is common in sports organizations. [34:49], [35:50]
- Transparency with the owner was the lesson one panelist took from his first year as GM. [39:26]
- Panelists said they mostly took accepted ideas to their logical conclusion (more threes, drafting stars). [40:58]
- A team without a singular edge that it resources is not differentiated. [43:04]
- Baseball is becoming a more efficient market, in a panelist's view, and football is not. [47:09]
- Panelists thought a GM could switch sports if the job is leadership and building a rational organization. [48:40]
- Chemistry: one panelist has never seen a winning team without it; the panel debated causal direction and suggested a virtuous or vicious cycle. [50:43], [54:49]
- Prediction of who will improve chemistry should carry low confidence. [55:49]
- Fans and owners can react negatively when a traded player does well elsewhere, which a panelist linked to loss aversion. [1:00:24]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Independent-decision reset.
- Secret-ballot grading and its limits.
- Written investment thesis with confidence, reread after two weeks.
- Reverse-the-trade check for endowment.
- Ordinal ranking of subjective scouting traits.
- Hypothesis test of a scout claim using a random video sample.
- Ground intelligence (scouts' local information).

## Limits and open questions

- Speaker attribution is uncertain in several passages.
- Examples are anecdotes from four organizations; no sample sizes or results were shown.
- The captions are garbled in places (e.g. titles, owner names).
- Claims about owner behavior, efficient markets and chemistry are the speakers' views.
- The panel did not resolve whether secret ballots help or hurt.
- Chemistry causality was left open.

## Q&A

- Could you switch sports as a GM? Panelists mostly said yes if the job is leadership and building rational process. [47:39]
- How does team chemistry relate to winning? Opinions varied; a virtuous or vicious cycle was proposed. [50:13]
- What is the most important issue for the community? One panelist said he was hopeful about the field and global growth. [56:49]
- Closing: loss aversion shocked one panelist when others viewed a former player's success elsewhere as a negative. [1:00:24]
